name: Johannesburg and Soweto
tagline: The City of Gold: a big, restless metropolis built on a gold rush, where the story of apartheid and the struggle to end it is told in museums and in the streets of Soweto.
highlight: Vilakazi Street in Soweto, where two Nobel Peace Prize winners lived a few doors apart.
shortDescription: South Africa's largest city and its historic heart: the Apartheid Museum, Constitution Hill, Soweto's Vilakazi Street and Hector Pieterson Memorial, urban renewal in Maboneng and the Cradle of Humankind.
metaDescription: A Johannesburg and Soweto travel guide: the Apartheid Museum, Constitution Hill, Vilakazi Street, Hector Pieterson Memorial, Orlando Towers, Maboneng, Cradle of Humankind, safety, where to stay and a two-day plan.
knownFor: Apartheid history, Soweto, gold-mining heritage, art and food, gateway to Kruger
goodFor: History, culture, food, art, business, a gateway city

image.alt: The skyline of the Johannesburg central business district with tall towers

intro: Johannesburg was founded in 1886, after gold was discovered on the Witwatersrand ridge, and it grew from a mining camp into a city of millions in a few decades. Known as Egoli, the place of gold, it is South Africa's largest city and its economic centre, at an altitude of about 1,750 metres. Despite its size and its reputation for crime, it is a city of energy, art, food and history, and one of the most important places for understanding modern South Africa.

Its history is inseparable from apartheid. The Apartheid Museum documents the rise and fall of racial segregation, and Constitution Hill, a former prison complex where Mahatma Gandhi and Nelson Mandela were held, now houses the Constitutional Court. Soweto, the South Western Townships, home to well over a million people, was the heart of the resistance. Vilakazi Street, where Mandela and Desmond Tutu lived, and the Hector Pieterson Memorial, commemorating the 1976 student uprising, are among its landmarks.

Johannesburg is best visited with local guidance, since central areas can be unsafe, but its neighbourhoods reward exploring. Maboneng and Braamfontein have galleries, cafés and markets, Melville and Rosebank have restaurants, and the Cradle of Humankind, a UNESCO site of fossil-bearing caves, lies an hour away. It is also the main gateway to Kruger and the north-east, and most visitors spend two days here at the start or end of a trip.

whyVisit.intro: Johannesburg and Soweto tell the story of modern South Africa, and offer urban culture that other cities lack.

points.title: The story of apartheid
points.text: The Apartheid Museum, Constitution Hill and Soweto are moving and essential.

points.title: Soweto
points.text: A living township with history, music, food and a proud community.

points.title: Urban culture
points.text: Art, markets, street food and nightlife in Maboneng, Braamfontein and Melville.

points.title: The Cradle of Humankind
points.text: Fossil caves where ancient hominid remains were found.

points.title: A gateway city
points.text: Connections to Kruger, Cape Town and the rest of Africa.

attractionsIntro: Most sights are best visited by ride-hailing or on a guided tour, and grouped by area.

attractions.name: The Apartheid Museum

image.alt: The entrance to the Apartheid Museum in Johannesburg with concrete pillars and a memorial

attractions.text: A superbly designed museum that traces the history of segregation and the struggle against it, with film, photographs and objects. Visitors enter through separate gates marked 'White' and 'Non-White'.

attractions.name: Constitution Hill

image.file: File:Flame of Democracy, Constitution Hill, Johannesburg.jpg
image.alt: The Flame of Democracy at Constitution Hill in Johannesburg

attractions.text: A former prison, called the Old Fort, and the site of the Constitutional Court, with museums and guided tours about the people who were held here, including Gandhi and Mandela.

attractions.name: Vilakazi Street and the Mandela House

image.alt: Street performers on Vilakazi Street in Soweto

attractions.text: The Soweto street where Nelson Mandela and Desmond Tutu both lived. The Mandela House is a museum, and the street has restaurants and performers.

attractions.name: Hector Pieterson Memorial and Museum
attractions.text: A memorial and museum to the 1976 Soweto student uprising, in which schoolchildren protested against apartheid education and many were killed.

attractions.name: Orlando Towers

image.alt: The painted cooling towers of the Orlando Power Station in Soweto

attractions.text: Two colourfully painted former power station cooling towers, now an adventure venue with bungee, swing and climbing, and a symbol of Soweto.

attractions.name: Maboneng Precinct

image.alt: A colourful art installation in the Maboneng precinct of Johannesburg

attractions.text: A revitalised inner-city district of warehouses, galleries, cafés and a Sunday market.
attractions.tip: Go on a Sunday, and use ride-hailing apps.

thingsToDoIntro: Combine history, food and urban culture.

thingsToDo.title: Take a guided Soweto tour
thingsToDo.text: A local guide shows the history, homes, markets and music.

thingsToDo.title: Eat at a shebeen or local restaurant
thingsToDo.text: Try kota sandwiches, braai and pap.

thingsToDo.title: Visit the Cradle of Humankind
thingsToDo.text: See the Sterkfontein Caves and the Maropeng exhibition, about 50 km away.

thingsToDo.title: See a jazz or live music show
thingsToDo.text: Johannesburg has a strong music scene.

thingsToDo.title: Shop at a market
thingsToDo.text: Neighbourhood Goods Market and Rosebank Rooftop Market.

thingsToDo.title: Go to a football match
thingsToDo.text: A game at FNB Stadium, where the 2010 World Cup final was played.

foodIntro: Johannesburg's food is diverse, from township street food to fine dining.

foods.name: Kota
foods.text: A Soweto street-food sandwich, a hollowed loaf filled with chips, egg, sausage and sauces.

foods.name: Braai and boerewors
foods.text: Grilled meat with pap and chakalaka relish.

foods.name: Pap and chakalaka
foods.text: Maize porridge with a spicy vegetable relish.

foods.name: Craft beer and coffee
foods.text: A strong café and craft beer scene.

accommodation.intro: Stay in Sandton, Rosebank or Melville for safety and convenience, or in a Soweto guesthouse.

areas.name: Sandton and Rosebank
areas.text: Business and leisure hotels near malls and the Gautrain.

gettingThere.intro: Johannesburg is South Africa's main international gateway.

options.text: Direct flights from Europe, the Middle East, Asia and North America, and across Africa.
options.detail: The Gautrain links the airport with Sandton.

gettingAround.intro: Use ride-hailing apps and tours, and avoid walking in unfamiliar areas.

options.text: The safest and easiest way to move.
A fast train linking the airport, Sandton, Rosebank and Pretoria.
Guided tours to Soweto and central areas.

bestTime.headline: April–October
bestTime.summary: Johannesburg has a mild highveld climate, with warm, wet summers and dry, sunny, cold-nighted winters.

seasons.text: Sunny, dry days and cold nights.

tipsIntro: A few tips help you stay safe and get the most out of the city.
tips: Use ride-hailing apps, and do not walk at night.
Do not go to the inner city without a guide.
Keep phones, cameras and jewellery out of sight.
Book a Soweto tour with a locally owned operator.
Allow plenty of time for the Apartheid Museum.
Lock car doors and windows when driving.

faq.q: How many days do you need in Johannesburg?
faq.a: Two days for the main sights, including Soweto.
Crime is a concern. Use ride-hailing apps, guided tours and reputable areas, and follow local advice.
Guided tours are generally safe and are a highlight of a visit.

faq.q: What is the best time to visit?
What is the Apartheid Museum like?
faq.a: It is powerful and sobering, and takes about three hours.

faq.q: Is it worth staying in Johannesburg?
faq.a: For two days, yes, for the history and culture.
